content: The exposure of mice to 1,1,1-trichloroethane did not affect ion levels. Administration of atropine, chlorpromazine, or tolazoline to mice immediately before and after 12 hours of exposure to 1,1,1-trichloroethane did not prevent the effects of the exposure on hexobarbital-induced sleeping time. A dose of 0 ml/kg did not enhance the hepatotoxicity of 1,1,1-trichloroethane, as assessed by serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) levels. Similar increases in SGOT levels were observed in both control animals (not pretreated with phenobarbital) and those treated with phenobarbital at each dose level of 1,1,1-trichloroethane. SGOT levels were significantly elevated by 1,1,1-trichloroethane exposure, regardless of phenobarbital pretreatment. Phenobarbital-induced enhancement of 1,1,1-trichloroethane hepatotoxicity was previously reported by Carlson in 1973. In that study, male rats were pretreated with phenobarbital (50 mg/kg/day) for four days before exposure. However, in this experiment, exposure of rats to redistilled reagent-grade 1,1,1-trichloroethane at concentrations of 10,000 or 15,000 ppm for 2 hours, or 5,000 or 10,000 ppm for 6 hours, did not result in increased serum enzyme levels, regardless of ethanol pretreatment. The serum enzymes studied in the 1966 report by Cornish and Adefuin included SGOT, serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT), and isocitric dehydrogenase. Ethanol (50%) was administered via stomach tube at 5 g/kg, 16–18 hours prior to vapor exposure. Pretreatment with isopropyl alcohol or acetone, administered by gavage to male Swiss-Webster mice 18 hours before intraperitoneal injection of 1,1,1-trichloroethane, did not alter the SGPT activity response to the administered 1,1,1-trichloroethane. A dose of 5 ml/kg caused increases in SGPT activity, but these increases were not influenced by pretreatment with isopropyl alcohol or acetone. The most significant findings regarding the effects of 1,1,1-trichloroethane in humans and animals include central nervous system (CNS) depression, cardiovascular toxicity, and hepatic toxicity. Irritation of the lungs and mucous membranes has also been reported. There is limited information on experimental exposures lasting more than six months or at concentrations below approximately 75 ppm. Both experimental studies and occupational experiences indicate that 1,1,1-trichloroethane is irritating to the skin and mucous membranes and that the nervous system, cardiovascular system, and liver are affected by exposure. The first biological study of 1,1,1-trichloroethane, conducted by Tauber in 1880, demonstrated its anesthetic properties. However, clinical trials between 1958 and 1960 established that it was not effective as a surgical anesthetic, leading to its discontinuation for this purpose. Despite this, its anesthetic properties have occupational significance and remain relevant to work practices and the use of respiratory protective devices. The concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane required to induce anesthesia under working conditions have not been determined. Clinical studies are difficult to extrapolate to occupational settings because patients were often sedated before administration of anesthetic gas, and nitrous oxide was used as a carrier gas for 1,1,1-trichloroethane. In dogs exposed to 1,1,1-trichloroethane at 8,000 ppm for no more than 5 minutes, cardiovascular changes included an abrupt drop in total peripheral resistance with compensatory cardiac responses. These compensatory responses dissipated within seconds, leading to decreases in stroke volume, heart rate, and myocardial contractility. Elevated urinary urobilinogen was observed in one subject following a 20-minute exposure at 900 ppm, and evidence of possible kidney injury was found in six subjects after exposure at 500 ppm for 78 minutes. Serum enzyme levels were not elevated. Evidence of kidney injury (red blood cells and protein in the urine) and elevated serum bilirubin were also observed in a man following ingestion of 1,1,1-trichloroethane. Elevated urinary urobilinogen was detected in one worker after working with 1,1,1-trichloroethane for one hour in a closed room and in two of nine women after several months of occupational exposure. Information on environmental concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane and engineering controls is limited. Concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane during cleaning of electrical equipment were reported by Burkatskaya et al. in 1973, but the sampling and analytical methods were not described. Greasy parts were sprayed with or dipped into the solvent, with spraying lasting 4–5 minutes and drying with an air jet for 2–3 minutes. The room had an exhaust fan and a general two-way exhaust system providing 35–40 air changes (time interval not specified). During spraying, concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane in the shop area ranged from 27 to 70 ppm, declining rapidly after the process was completed. After 30 minutes, room air concentrations were not measurable. Concentrations in different parts of the room during dipping tank operations ranged from 25 to 55 ppm. When parts were removed from the bath, approximately 250 ppm of 1,1,1-trichloroethane was detected in the workroom air. Workers were exposed to concentrations exceeding the threshold limit value (TLV) of 100 ppm throughout their working day.
